title: 'Thinking about my ute': How 12yo passed time on 16-day walk to meet PM

Topic:Charities

Dusty Langby celebrates with his family on arrival in Canberra. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

Dusty Langby has completed his 500-kilometre walk from his NSW hometown to raise money for the charity Little Wings, which provides flights for rural children who need specialist appointments.

Dusty and his crew braved rain and baking sunshine over the course of their 16-day journey, navigating mental and physical challenges.

The prime minister has agreed to match the funds raised by Dusty for Little Wings, donating $500,000 to the cause.

Twelve-year-old Dusty Langby has made it to Canberra, completing a 500-kilometre, 16-day walk from his hometown in western New South Wales and raising more than $500,000 to deliver paediatric care to bush communities.

To top off the long journey, Dusty met with the prime minister to discuss that same topic.

"When we were walking to Canberra today, we saw there were flags at the top of parliament," Dusty told 666 ABC Canberra.

Supporters line the path on day one, as the crew make their way to Trangie from Warren, NSW. (Supplied)

The trek began in Dusty's hometown, Warren, NSW, on August 30, with his crew comprising his mum Sarah, local nurse Christine Letton, Little Wings nurse Nichole Callan, and Little Wings chief executive Clare Pearson.

The charity Little Wings provides free flights for children who are seriously ill, or who need specialist care in rural and regional NSW, ACT and Queensland.

Both Dusty and his brother have flown from Warren to Sydney with Little Wings for specialist medical appointments.

"It's just such an amazing cause," Dusty said, wanting more children to be able to access the service.

Dusty said he wanted more children to access the services of Little Wings charity. (Supplied)

"The pilots and the volunteers are such kind people, and they all are just really kind, and I wanted to help."

On his agenda for his appointment with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Dusty said, was asking the PM to match every dollar he has raised for the charity.

At the time of finishing his walk, he had raised $423,000, which he said was "going to change heaps of rural families' lives" and "just help more kids".

By Tuesday, more than $500,000 had been raised for Little Wings and Mr Albanese agreed to match the donations.

For Dusty, committing to the mission meant slowing down and finding a hobby in walking.

"I don't really walk; I normally run. So it took me a long time to get used to walking, not running," he said.

At some stages, Dusty thought about his ute to pass the time. (Supplied)

That involved training since January on walks, which overall ate through four pairs of shoes, he recalled.

Over the course of the trip, with each day ranging from a 19 to a 55 kilometre-long commute, the team's energy levels ebbed and flowed.

"At the start we were just chatting all the way, we weren't listening to music, we were just chatting away," he said.

"I think it was the third day where we started to walk in silence.

The family will go camping to 'decompress' and take in Dusty's achievement. (Supplied)

Sometimes he passed the time by planning upgrades to his 1999 Toyota Hilux ute.

"My pop has some lights I'm going to put on the ute, so I was just thinking about that," he said.

His mum, Sarah, said every day had been different.

Dusty and his mum Sarah say each day varied from the next as they walked from town to town towards Canberra. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

"But all rewarding in itself, each day and every community we enter just welcomed us so gracefully and so humbling, and we are just amazed," she said.

Ms Langby said they had many supporters cheering them on, and offering them food at each leg.

She gave shout-outs to the people, pubs and inns of Yass, Murrumbateman, Parkes, and the Lake Cargelligo school, which delivered the crew a Woolworths order.

"There's just so many we can't even [thank them enough], and express our gratitude for feeding us beautiful and nutritious food for the trip," Ms Langby said.

Now in Canberra, Dusty said his feet have been spared from blisters, and he was feeling "really good" after the 16-day mission.

The family will go camping together, Ms Langby said, to take in Dusty's huge feat.

"We're going to decompress, just have a bit of time with Dad, my other son Angus, just being on the river fishing, motorbike riding, and just enjoy our company and reflect on what we've just achieved," she said.
